_comment: Hand-written fixture data backing the stub tools. Domain vocabulary lives here, in data, never in code. Record ids are real-format 24-hex ObjectId strings so downstream links are shaped like the real thing. `similarity` is present on records so the stub can bucket it into relatedness and report the raw number to the trace. IMPORTANT: summaries and excerpts name what a record is ABOUT and never what happened in it — a summary that states the conclusion removes the agent's reason to open the record, which is the constraint the whole loop depends on. Keep the diagnosis in `content` only.

records.summary: Interview debrief. System design round, rate limiting question with a follow-up on algorithm choice.
records.content:
Second round, system design. The prompt was rate limiting for a public API.
I opened with token bucket and covered bucket capacity and refill rate. The interviewer pushed: "what about leaky bucket, when would you reach for that?"
I said leaky bucket smooths bursts by flattening spiky traffic. He didn't respond, just asked "can't token bucket smooth bursts too?" I stalled, mumbled "token bucket is more flexible" and stopped.
Looked it up afterwards. Both handle bursts; the real difference is that token bucket lets a burst through once tokens have accumulated, while leaky bucket forces a constant output rate. I had attached the word "smoothing" to the wrong one.

records.summary: Interview debrief. System design round, cache penetration question with a follow-up.
records.content:
Got asked about cache penetration. I said use a bloom filter to reject keys that don't exist.
Interviewer asked "anything else?" I drew a blank. He hinted "what if the lookup comes back empty?" and only then did I say cache the empty value.
Feels like I've read this but it isn't reflexive yet. One follow-up and I freeze.

records.summary: Interview debrief. System design round, database sharding question with a follow-up on resharding.
records.content:
Sharding question went fine.
Started with hashing on user id, then raised unprompted that sharding by time creates a hotspot because the newest shard takes all the write pressure.
Interviewer nodded and asked about resharding. I covered consistent hashing and dual-write migration. Counting this one as a pass.

records.summary: Saved article, "Rate Limiting in Practice", covering the common rate limiting algorithms.
records.content:
Rate Limiting in Practice

Token bucket and leaky bucket are the pair most often conflated, and the difference comes down to how each one treats a burst.
Leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate. Bursts queue inside the bucket and the output curve stays flat — it trades burst responsiveness for absolute downstream stability.
Token bucket instead lets a burst through in one go once enough tokens have accrued, as long as the long-run average stays within budget. For a user-facing API, token bucket is almost always the better fit.

records.summary: Study log. Hands-on work on a rate limiting implementation and its parameters.
records.content:
Wrote a token bucket limiter with Redis and Lua.
Bucket capacity decides how large a burst you can absorb, refill rate decides long-run throughput, and they are two separate knobs — I had been thinking of it as a single "rate limit" number.
Load tested with capacity 100 and rate 10/s. The first 100 requests all went through instantly, then it settled to 10 per second. Burst behaviour and steady-state behaviour are obvious once you watch it.

records.summary: Study log. Reading notes on the CAP theorem.
records.content: CAP: consistency, availability, partition tolerance. Partition tolerance isn't optional in a distributed system, so the real choice is CP or AP.
